name: Avoiding ultra-processed foods
lead: Avoiding ultra-processed foods (UPFs) is a whole-food dietary approach, sometimes used by people trying to lose fat, based on the NOVA food classification, in which UPFs are industrially manufactured products made from many ingredients, often including additives and ingredients rarely used in home cooking. [1]
Observational studies link high UPF intake with obesity and chronic disease, while critics say the category is poorly defined and that randomised evidence is limited. [1]
infobox: Carlos Monteiro and colleagues, University of Sao Paulo, 2009 [1]

paras: NOVA sorts foods into four groups by degree of processing. Brazilian researcher Carlos Augusto Monteiro and colleagues described it in 2009. NOVA considers ingredients, processing and marketing rather than nutrient content. [1] Brazil, Uruguay, Peru and Ecuador have dietary guidelines advising avoidance of UPFs, and Chile requires warning labels on some. [1]

Epidemiological studies associate UPF consumption with obesity, poorer cardiometabolic and mental health and reduced life expectancy. A 2023 meta-analysis found 12 percent higher type 2 diabetes risk per 10 percent increase in intake, and a 2025 meta-analysis found 15 percent higher all-cause mortality for the highest versus lowest consumers. Associations differ by subgroup, with cereals and bread showing inverse links. [1]

Critics, including Arne Astrup, say the concept is ambiguous, relies on observational data and may overlook beneficial processing. The one frequently cited randomised trial does not control for macronutrient profile or energy density, and the obesity link has not been confirmed by randomised trials. The UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition recommended further research rather than adopting a position. [1] A study of grain fortification in Australia found that avoiding UPFs could alter nutrient intakes, because many fortified breads and cereals are classed as UPFs yet are recommended core foods. [2]
No studies found testing UPF avoidance specifically for appearance outcomes. Observational and meta-analytic evidence on health outcomes is summarised above. [1]

timeline.event: Monteiro and colleagues describe the NOVA classification. [1]

refs.title: Fortification of grain foods and NOVA: the potential for altered nutrient intakes while avoiding ultra-processed foods

card.summary: A whole-food approach built on the NOVA scheme; linked to health outcomes in observational studies but no appearance trials.
card.note: The UPF category is contested by some nutrition researchers.

quick.overview:
This approach means cutting industrially manufactured, multi-ingredient foods and eating mostly whole or minimally processed ones, often to reduce body fat.

Observational studies link UPFs to obesity and disease, but the category itself is debated.
quick.mechanism: NOVA classifies foods by processing rather than nutrients. Mechanisms linking UPFs to harm are described as unclear.
quick.risks: Little direct risk reported. One study noted that avoiding UPFs could change nutrient intake, since fortified breads and cereals are often classed as UPFs.
